title: Churchgoing couples have more sex, greater sexual satisfaction, new report finds | Institute for Family Studies
gist: A Christian Post write-up of the IFS report 'The Devout Difference' says regularly churchgoing, praying married couples report more frequent and more satisfying sex than secular couples. Secular couples show the global 'sex recession' pattern while devout Christian couples have largely resisted it.

insights.claim: An Institute for Family Studies report finds that married couples who attend church regularly, pray often and hold traditional beliefs such as marriage being a lifelong commitment have more frequent and better sex than secular couples.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Religious practice is linked to relationship stability and household formation, both of which shape long-run demand and demographics.
insights.quote: Husbands and wives who attend church regularly, pray often and embrace their faith’s classic teachings, including the belief that marriage is a life commitment, have more and better sex than their secular peers
insights.locator: Husbands and wives who attend church

insights.claim: Adults worldwide have been having sex much less often over the past few decades, a trend called the 'sex recession', and secular US couples show the same decline.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Less partnering and intimacy feeds into falling fertility, fewer households and more loneliness, which together shape consumer and housing demand.
insights.locator: In its report, The Devout Difference

insights.claim: According to IFS researchers, churchgoing Christian couples have largely resisted the 'sex recession', so religiosity appears to protect against the broader drop in sexual activity.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Demographic and fertility trends may increasingly split along religious lines, so religious subgroups may end up a larger share of future population.
insights.quote: churchgoing Christian couples have largely been resilient against it
insights.locator: In its report, The Devout Difference

insights.claim: A related news item on the IFS page reports that unhappiness and isolation are rising among young people, while religious young people are doing well.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Loneliness among young people is a social trend that affects consumer behaviour, mental-health spending and family formation.
insights.quote: Unhappiness and Isolation Are Rising among Young People, but Those Who Are Religious Are Thriving
